To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the estimated HIV prevalence among construction workers is lower than previously estimated, that HIV prevalence is associated with gender, age, occupation, and nature of employment, and that HIV testing history is associated with HIV prevalence.

(i) HIV infection among construction workers is lower than previously estimated, but (ii) HIV infection among female construction workers is higher than among males, and (iii) construction workers who are not in permanent employment are at a higher risk of HIV infection, and (iv) HIV testing is a significant predictor of HIV serostatus.
HIV prevalence is lower than in a 2008 sample, and that females, older, more casual, and less recently tested workers, and workers in certain occupations are most at risk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of vulnerable groups in the construction industry for the purposes of HIV workplace interventions.
the identification of the most at risk groups of construction workers in South Africa, in order to target interventions at those groups.
the construction of a more comprehensive and accurate picture of the nature and scale of the problem of HIV in the South African context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the South African construction sector is a high-risk sector in which HIV infection is prevalent.
construction workers are more at risk from HIV than other sectors in the South African economy.
the HIV infection rate among construction workers is lower than that of the general population, but that the construction workforce is not homogeneous in this respect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HIV infection rate among construction workers is high and that the industry has a high proportion of at-risk workers.
the construction industry is not a particularly high risk industry for HIV, but that it is a microcosm of the general South African population in terms of its HIV prevalence.

the HIV prevalence of construction workers in South Africa is lower than previously estimated, and that there is a strong association between worker characteristics and HIV infection, which should be taken into consideration when developing HIV workplace programmes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

construction firms should be encouraged to implement workplace HIV interventions that are tailored to their workforce characteristics, and to do so in a manner that is consistent with their own organizational culture.
HIV prevalence among the construction workforce in South Africa is higher than the general population, and the prevalence is increasing.
the construction industry in South Africa, as a major economic sector, has a significant role to play in the national effort to reduce HIV infections and to improve the health of its workforce.
